title: Chronic pain
hook: long pain can be carried with others
tomorrow: what could possibly be missing from Christ's sufferings?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: not a punishment, neither this man nor his parents. But some pain doesn't pass in a week.

A grandmother who has folded tamales for years, wincing only when she thinks nobody's looking. Long pain gets quiet. You stop mentioning it because it never changes, and people stop asking. Now, a house in Capernaum, so packed nobody can get through the door. Inside, Jesus is teaching. And above everyone's heads, the roof starts to come apart. Dust falls. Daylight. Four men are up there, digging.
screen: `LONG PAIN GETS QUIET.` → `A HOUSE TOO FULL TO ENTER.` → `FOUR MEN ON THE ROOF.`

segments.voice: Mark explains, in the Douay-Rheims: "And they came to him, bringing one sick of the palsy, who was carried by four." The man can't walk. The crowd won't move. So his friends open the roof and lower his bed right down in front of Jesus. Then a small line with a big turn: "And when Jesus had seen their faith." One to tell a friend: it's their faith, the four friends', that Jesus sees first. The man on the bed didn't have to carry his own hope down through the ceiling. Not every long pain in scripture lifts. Paul writes of a sting in his flesh that he begged God to take away, and the answer he got was, "My grace is sufficient for thee: for power is made perfect in infirmity." The pain stayed. So did the grace. That's why Catholics ask each other for prayers, put names on parish prayer lists, and have Masses offered for the sick. Paul says it plainly to the Galatians: "Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ." Chronic pain may not be fixable. It's still meant to be carried by more than one.
screen: `CARRIED BY FOUR.` · `WHEN JESUS HAD SEEN THEIR FAITH.` · `MY GRACE IS SUFFICIENT.` · `BEAR YE ONE ANOTHER'S BURDENS.` · then, large: `CARRIED TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Think of one person you trust. Send them a short message asking them to pray for you, or to keep you in mind, about one thing that's been heavy a long time. You don't have to explain it all; the four on the roof never gave a speech. Then sit quietly while it goes.
Chronic pain. Pain that lasts and lasts, which this tradition says no one should have to carry alone. Today's word.
Your line: carried together, four friends and a hole in the roof. See you tomorrow.

fork.setup: a teammate has had migraines for two years. she's stopped mentioning them, and stopped coming to team dinners. what do the four on the roof suggest?
options: ask what helps, and make the plan around her, not without her.
wait until she asks; bringing it up might embarrass her.
tell her about a cure you read about so she can finally fix it.
fork.reveal: the four didn't fix the man; they carried him where help was. long pain gets quiet, so friends go first.

original.note: Greek: lasting a long time, from chronos, time. the English word chronic comes from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: chronic pain is something you deal with privately.
what it means: this tradition says long pain is carried together, by prayer, presence and practical help.
what a scholar hears: Mark 2:3–5 (their faith); 2 Corinthians 12:7–9 (Paul's 'sting of my flesh' in the Douay-Rheims); Galatians 6:2.
guess: pain that lasts a long time and doesn't go away
a sudden injury that heals within a few days
a punishment that lasts until you repent

chat.says: abuela brought me soup and i saw her hands. swollen. dad says they've hurt for years. she never said.
options: Ask what helps, and offer to pray or carry things. Long pain isn't solo.
Leave it. If she wanted help with it, she'd have asked by now.
Tell her to pray harder. If she has enough faith, it'll heal.
chat.meaning: Jesus saw the faith of the four who carried their friend. Long pain gets quiet, so the people around it go first.

Capernaum.meaning: a fishing town by the Sea of Galilee where Jesus taught

palsy.meaning: older English for paralysis, being unable to move

Galatians.meaning: Christians in Galatia, to whom Paul wrote a letter

notes: Mark 2:3, 2:5, 2 Corinthians 12:9 and Galatians 6:2 quoted from Douay-Rheims; confirm exact wording.
Mark 2:1 places the scene at Capharnaum (Douay spelling); the house being packed and the roof uncovered are in Mark 2:2–4. Confirm.
Paul's 'sting of my flesh' (2 Cor 12:7, Douay) paraphrased as 'a sting in his flesh'; that he asked three times is in the text but omitted. 'The pain stayed' is a reading of 12:9; confirm framing.
